topic: Space-Filling Curves: Folding a Line into a Square
target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Mathematics, or Physics)

sections.title: The Dimensionality Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the mind-bending question: Can a one-dimensional line occupy every single point in a two-dimensional square? We transition from the intuitive concept of a 'thin line' to a 'dense map'.
sections.example: Imagine a tiny, infinitely thin 'Quantum Snail' leaving a trail. Can it crawl in such a way that no part of the garden floor is left untouched?

sections.title: Prerequisite: Iteration and Limits
sections.content: Explain the concept of 'Iterative Functions' and 'Limits'. To understand space-filling curves, one must understand that the 'curve' is the result of a process repeated an infinite number of times.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Level 1' square divided into 4 quadrants, then each quadrant divided again ('Level 2'), creating a nested grid structure.

sections.title: The Hilbert Curve Construction
sections.content: Step-by-step visual assembly of the Hilbert Curve. Define the 'U-shape' generator and show how it rotates and connects as the iteration level (n) increases from 1 to 4.
sections.example: Show a simple 'U' shape (n=1). At n=2, four smaller 'U' shapes appear, rotated and linked by three segments. By n=5, the line looks like a solid block of color.

sections.title: Mathematical Mapping: [0, 1] → [0, 1]²
sections.content: Explain the mapping function f(t) = (x, y). For every point on a number line between 0 and 1, there is a corresponding (x, y) coordinate in the square. Emphasize 'Surjectivity' (covering everything) and 'Continuity' (no lifting the pen).
sections.example: A slider moving from 0.0 to 1.0 on a timeline. As the slider moves, a cursor moves continuously across the 2D grid without ever jumping.

sections.title: Key Property: Locality Preservation
sections.content: Highlight why space-filling curves are useful: points that are close together on the 1D line tend to be close together in the 2D plane. This is the 'Clustering' property.
sections.example: A robot vacuum using a Hilbert path to clean a room. Because the path preserves locality, the robot cleans one corner thoroughly before moving to the next, rather than zig-zagging randomly.

sections.title: Modern Applications: From Maps to Data
sections.content: Demonstrate how this abstract math solves real-world problems like image compression, range queries in databases (SQL/NoSQL), and Google Maps' 'S2' geometry library.
sections.example: Visualizing how a high-resolution 2D image is flattened into a 1D string of data for fast transmission while keeping neighboring pixels together to improve compression ratios.
